titulo.texto: Manuel Tolsá Plaza and El Caballito

frase_gancho.texto: A bronze Spanish king who survived Independence, changed places several times, and is known by everyone by the name of his horse.

puente_narrativo.texto: Cross Tacuba Street toward the Palace of Mining, the neoclassical building with columns across the way, facing this plaza.

como_llegar.texto: Continue along Tacuba Street, just a few steps, toward the neighboring plaza, where the equestrian sculpture known as El Caballito stands.

guion_corto.texto: Nobody says Charles the Fourth. To the whole city, this bronze sculpture is El Caballito, a nickname that honors the horse and not the king. The rider appears dressed as a Roman emperor. The work is by Manuel Tolsá, a sculptor and architect from Valencia. It was made to honor the Spanish monarch in the Plaza Mayor, where it was placed in eighteen oh three. The inscription on its base states that it was cast in Mexico City, and that horse and rider came out of a single pour. After Independence the statue came close to being destroyed. It changed location more than once and arrived here in nineteen seventy-nine, in front of the Palace of Mining, another work by Tolsá.

guion_largo.texto:
The story of El Caballito begins where the Zócalo is today. There, in the old Plaza Mayor, it was placed in eighteen oh three. The inscription on its base says that the statue was cast and poured in Mexico on the fourth of August, eighteen oh two, and that it was placed in the plaza on the ninth of December, eighteen oh three. It was dedicated by the viceroy Miguel de la Grúa Talamanca, Marquis of Branciforte. Before that there had been a provisional wooden version, from seventeen ninety-six.

Behind the work is Manuel Tolsá. He was born in Valencia, trained as a sculptor, and in New Spain he was also an architect and director of sculpture at the Academy of San Carlos. His challenge was technical. The casting was done at the Colegio de San Gregorio, and rider and horse came out of a single pour, something the plaque on the pedestal records. After that came fourteen months of chiseling and polishing.

Moving the bronze was also a feat. From the casting site to the Plaza Mayor the statue traveled about one thousand six hundred meters, and the transfer took five days. The naturalist Alexander von Humboldt was present and described as very ingenious the mechanisms with which they raised it onto the pedestal of Mexican marble.

When Mexico became independent, a statue of a Spanish king became an awkward presence. Some people called for it to be torn down and melted. Intellectuals and politicians such as Lucas Alamán defended its artistic value, and thanks to that it was preserved.

In eighteen twenty-two it was covered, and in eighteen twenty-four it was taken to the courtyard of the Royal and Pontifical University. It was no longer in the main plaza. In eighteen fifty-two it was moved to the intersection of Reforma and Bucareli, on a new pedestal designed by Lorenzo de la Hidalga. And in nineteen seventy-nine it arrived at this plaza, which bears the name of its author.

That is why El Caballito sums up a good part of the history of Mexico. It was a viceregal commission, then an awkward symbol, and later a piece defended for its artistic value. Not even the nickname refers to the king, but to the horse.

The plaza where you are standing has its own history too. Here were the gardens of the old Palace of Communications, which today is the MUNAL. When it arrived in nineteen seventy-nine, the statue ended up between two buildings from very different eras. One is Tolsá's neoclassical building, from the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The other is the Porfirian palace, from the early twentieth century.

The bronze has also suffered in recent times. In two thousand thirteen, an intervention carried out without specialists damaged its surface with an acid. Between two thousand sixteen and two thousand seventeen, the INAH restored it.

Now look toward the Palace of Mining, the neoclassical building that Tolsá directed for almost sixteen years. The plaza thus brings together his two trades, that of sculptor and that of architect. When you later reach the Zócalo, remember that this bronze once stood there before beginning its long walk through the city.

texto: Look for the inscriptions on the base of the statue and read what they say
Notice the rider’s cloak and how its folds fall over the horse’s back
Find the columned portico with a triangular pediment on the Palace of Mining, the work of Tolsá himself

texto.Period: Cast on August 4, 1802 and placed on December 9, 1803 in the Plaza Mayor
texto.Author: Manuel Tolsá, sculptor and architect
texto.Material: Bronze, cast in a single pour
texto.Key fact: In this plaza since 1979, after stops at the University and at Reforma and Bucareli

texto.pregunta: Myth: El Caballito is a sculpture brought from Spain.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was made in Mexico City by Manuel Tolsá, and it was cast in a single pour at the Colegio de San Gregorio.
